\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Why per-DOF conformal features fail.}
At $K{=}10$ samples in $d{=}6$ dimensions, per-DOF statistics carry substantial estimation noise despite Ledoit--Wolf shrinkage~\cite{ledoit2004well}.
The frozen observation embedding $\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{obs}} \in \mathbb{R}^{960}$ already encodes the geometric information these features attempt to capture.
Adding noisy low-dimensional statistics to this rich representation degrades CRM predictions rather than improving them.
A subtler issue is the gap between offline and closed-loop metrics: all CRM variants achieve low per-step MSE on held-out data, yet offline accuracy does not predict closed-loop success.
In closed-loop execution, compounding error~\cite{ross2011dagger} shifts the state distribution, and noisy conformal features amplify this drift.

\paragraph{Selection vs.\ correction: contrast with LLM scaling.}
Test-time compute scaling in LLMs relies primarily on selection: generating multiple candidates and choosing the best via a verifier or reward model~\cite{snell2024scaling}.
Our component decomposition reveals the opposite pattern in embodied action spaces.
Random selection at $K{=}10$ performs at the VLA-only level ($11.7$\% vs.\ $11.6$\%), and argmin selection adds a statistically insignificant margin ($12.3$\% vs.\ $11.7$\%).
The entire +6.0\,pp pipeline improvement is attributable to learned CRM correction.
The structural explanation is that continuous action spaces are low-dimensional ($d{=}6$), so $K{=}10$ flow-matching samples cluster tightly around the mode; selection among near-identical candidates offers negligible discriminative power.
Learned correction, by contrast, exploits the 960-dimensional observation embedding to predict a directed residual toward the expert action, a mechanism unavailable to pure selection.
This finding suggests that transferring test-time compute ideas from language to embodied domains requires rethinking the selection-correction balance: in action spaces, the value of repeated sampling lies not in picking winners but in providing a stable starting point for learned refinement.

\paragraph{When does action-level correction help?}
The +6.0\,pp gain on LIBERO-Object versus the null result on LIBERO-Spatial reveals a structural distinction.
Object perturbations create systematic action biases that a learned module can compensate from observation features.
Spatial perturbations require higher-level re-planning; action-level residuals cannot redirect toward a different goal location.
The benefit of post-hoc correction depends on whether the distribution shift manifests as correctable motor error or as a planning-level failure.
